meta.title: Will the AI bubble pop before 2030?
meta.description: 'Pop' means a broad, lasting repricing of AI equities and infrastructure before 1 January 2030 — the kind of drawdown that ends a capital-spending cycle, not a correction. The model asks three things: is spending outrunning revenue, does the macro environment turn hostile, and do frontier capabilities stall? A probability table combines them, a mixture gives the size of the drawdown in each world, and a small allocation decision shows what the uncertainty is worth to a portfolio. Numbers are 2026 judgments; replace them with sourced priors as connectors arrive.

nodes.title: AI capital spending growth, 2026–2028
nodes.notes: Annual growth in data-centre, chip, and power spending by the hyperscalers and their suppliers, as a fraction per year. Hyperscaler capex roughly doubled between 2023 and 2025; the median here assumes it keeps growing but slows. The P90 is a continued boom, the P10 a stall.

nodes.title: AI revenue growth, 2026–2028
nodes.notes: Annual growth in revenue actually attributable to AI products — inference, subscriptions, enterprise contracts — as a fraction per year. Growing fast from a small base, so the spread is wide.

nodes.title: Spending growth minus revenue growth
nodes.notes: Positive means capital is being deployed faster than revenue is arriving to pay for it. Bubbles are made of this gap persisting.

nodes.title: Overbuild: spending outruns revenue by more than 10 points a year
nodes.notes: A threshold on the gap. Ten percentage points a year, sustained for three years, is a large hole to fill.

nodes.title: Rate or liquidity shock before 2030
nodes.notes: A sharp tightening of financial conditions — rates up, credit spreads out — inside the window. Roughly the base rate of a recession-grade shock in any four-year span.

nodes.title: Frontier capabilities plateau by 2028
nodes.notes: No step change in what models can do between now and 2028: scaling returns flatten and the story shifts from 'what will it do next' to 'what does it cost'. A plateau removes the narrative that justifies the spend.

nodes.title: The bubble pops before 2030
nodes.notes: Probability of a pop for each combination of overbuild, rate shock, and plateau. Overbuild is the main driver; a shock or a plateau on top of it makes a pop likely; without overbuild, even a shock mostly produces a correction rather than a bust.

nodes.title: Peak-to-trough fall in AI equities by 2030
nodes.notes: Fraction lost from the peak, bounded on both sides because a position cannot lose more than everything. In a pop, the 2000–2002 Nasdaq (down 78%) is near the far end and a 30% fall the mild end, with the most likely outcome a little over half. Without a pop, ordinary volatility: a shakeout most likely around 12%, at worst 40%.

nodes.title: Fall worse than 50%
nodes.notes: The dot-com benchmark: a fall that halves the sector.

nodes.title: AI equity return to 2030 if there is no pop
nodes.notes: Cumulative return on an AI basket from 2026 to 2030 in the worlds where the cycle holds: modest to spectacular.

nodes.title: Cumulative bond return to 2030
nodes.notes: What the money earns if it is not in AI equities.

nodes.title: AI equity return to 2030
nodes.notes: In a pop, the position ends at the trough; otherwise it earns the boom return. Simplified on purpose — no rebalancing, no partial recovery.

nodes.title: Stay fully in AI, or move half to bonds?
Portfolio return on the chosen allocation
nodes.notes: Alternatives are indexed in order, so `allocation` is 0 for stay_in and 1 for trim_half.

nodes.title: Log utility of final wealth
nodes.notes: Log utility penalises the chance of a large loss more than it rewards the chance of a large gain — which is the whole reason the answer can differ from the expected return.
